title: Computational Challenges in Probabilistic Knowledge Graph Traversal
description: This discussion focuses on the computational difficulties encountered when performing knowledge graph completion or traversal on dense graphs with probabilistic links. The core challenge lies in managing the exponential growth of search space caused by combining probabilistic expansions across query steps.
summary: The central problem discussed is the computational expense of knowledge graph completion and traversal when dealing with new, probabilistic edges. Specifically, the speaker highlights that traversing a query—moving from one entity along a relation to a set of nodes, and then to the next relation—results in an exponential increase in the search space based on the query length ($L$). This exponential expansion makes performing large queries on massive knowledge graphs ($N$) computationally hard. The task involves not only finding valid paths but also accurately tracking and managing these new probabilistic computing edges, which constitutes a very difficult computational task.

title: Handling Path Queries in Structured Data Systems
description: This segment discusses how systems can answer complex path queries using logical formulas or graphical structures, emphasizing the ability to answer any query at test time without needing to train on specific query-answer pairs. It also highlights the requirement for accurate transcription of speech segments.
summary: The discussion focuses on designing systems capable of handling queries in various formats, such as natural language, logical formulas, or graphical structures. The core idea is that once a logical structure is established, the system can answer any path query defined by a set of relations. Crucially, the method allows the system to answer any query at test time, rather than requiring specific training examples for each query. Finally, the method mandates that the system must be able to accurately transcribe the speech segment in its original language.

title: Knowledge Graph Querying and Path Traversal
description: This text discusses how to formulate and execute various types of queries (one-hop and path queries) on knowledge graphs using natural language, demonstrating how to traverse specific entity-relation paths to find answers.
summary: The segment explains the methodology for querying knowledge graphs, distinguishing between one-hop queries, which start with an entity and move across a single relation, and longer path queries. It illustrates complex path queries by chaining multiple relations (e.g., Entity A -> Relation 1 -> Entity B -> Relation 2 -> Entity C) to find a final answer. Specific examples are provided, such as finding proteins associated with adverse events caused by a drug (by traversing 'causes' and 'associated' relations), and identifying common drugs based on treating and causing specific conditions, demonstrating how natural language questions map to structured graph traversals.

title: Knowledge Graph Completion for Biomedical Queries
description: This topic discusses the challenge of answering complex queries over incomplete biomedical knowledge graphs by leveraging knowledge graph completion techniques. The goal is to estimate missing links to find answers, even when exhaustive traversal is computationally infeasible.
summary: The context introduces a biomedical knowledge graph containing nodes for drugs, diseases, adverse events, and proteins. The main problem is how to answer complex queries, such as finding all side effects caused by a specific drug. While a complete graph would allow simple traversal, real-world biomedical graphs are notoriously incomplete, making it impossible to enumerate all possible facts. Specifically, finding indirect answers requires bridging missing links. Knowledge graph completion is introduced as the solution method, which allows for estimating the existence of a link (head $\rightarrow$ relation $\rightarrow$ tail) to predict missing facts and enable the retrieval of complex answers over incomplete biomedical data.

title: Multi-Hop Reasoning and Logical Inference in Knowledge Graphs using Embeddings
description: This lecture introduces the methods for performing multi-hop and logical reasoning over knowledge graphs (KGs) by leveraging embeddings. The primary goal is to enable the system to answer complex, multi-step queries or make sophisticated predictions within the knowledge graph structure.
summary: The lecture focuses on performing multi-hop and logical reasoning within knowledge graphs using embeddings. The core objective of this reasoning is to enable the system to answer complex multi-hop queries or make complex predictions for arbitrary predictive queries. The planned topics for reasoning over KGs include answering multi-hop queries, path queries, conjunctive queries, and Query2box. A key shift discussed is moving the prediction task from a simple one-step prediction to a multi-step prediction task, where the goal is to identify which entities serve as the answer to a query rather than just answering the query directly.

title: Predictive Queries over Incomplete Knowledge Graphs
description: This work addresses the challenge of answering path-based queries over incomplete knowledge graphs by developing a method to implicitly predict and impute missing relationships. The goal is to create a robust approach that can traverse the graph without explicitly needing to fill every missing edge.
summary: The segment introduces the concept of a knowledge graph completion task focused on predicting missing relationships to enable the answering of path-based queries. While standard traversal methods assume a complete graph, which is unrealistic given that knowledge graphs are notoriously incomplete (lacking many relations). Therefore, the proposed approach is to define "predictive queries" that implicitly impute or complete the knowledge graph for missing information. This method aims to make the query answering robust to graph noise and incompleteness. The task is framed as a generalization of the link prediction task (Head + Relation $\rightarrow$ Tail), where the objective is to infer the missing tails such that path-based queries can still be answered effectively.

title: Defining and Traversing End-Hop Path Queries
description: This segment introduces the structure of an end-hop path query (Q) using a watisgolden anchor node and a sequence of relations. It outlines a method for querying data by traversing specific link types (green vs. red links) to arrive at a target protein.
summary: The discussion defines an end-hop path query Q, which is represented by a watisgolden anchor node (a starting entity) followed by a sequence of relations (R1 to RN). A key component is the anchor node, which is described as a fixed entity, such as a fullvest strand. The notation for answers utilizes double braces. The method for traversing the path involves first reviewing the 'green links' (which indicate what causes something) and then traversing the second part of the link to reach the desired protein, which forms the core idea for executing path queries.

title: Querying Knowledge Graphs through Embedding and Path Prediction
description: This discussion focuses on how to embed knowledge graphs to enable reasoning and navigation. It introduces a method for answering complex queries by formulating them as predictions, moving beyond simple link prediction to generalized path queries.
summary: The lecture introduces the use of conjunctive queries and a method called "query to box" to address how to embed knowledge graphs (KGs) and relations for reasoning and navigation. Initially, the discussion focuses on answering one-hop queries, such as simple link prediction or knowledge graph completion. The core idea then generalizes this to answering path queries, which involves chaining multiple relations. This is formalized by creating a "query plan" that specifies a traversal starting from an initial entity, moving across specific relationship types, and identifying the final entities. Ultimately, the entire process is framed as a prediction task: predicting what entities serve as the answer to a given query on the knowledge graph.
